muttHero: ↶ Home Field Manual MTH-1 · all mail clients suck; this one less mutt — From Nothing to Hero One config file, one key language, IMAP in, SMTP out, several providers at once and colors everywhere. This page is the road: nothing to hero, the four files that matter, and the two hooks (folder-hook, account-hook) that make several mailboxes behave. muttrc · mailboxes · IMAP · SMTP · Gmail vanilla JS · CSS3 · no dependencies passwords stay out of the page and yours 01 From nothing mutt is a terminal email client with a slogan older than the dot-com bubble and still true: “All mail clients suck. This one just sucks less.” It was written in 1995 by Michael Elkins, forked decades later into neomutt , and remains the email program people reach for when they finally want to triage their inbox faster than a pointer can move. It is keyboard-native. Every action is a key; every key is a line in your config. Nothing hidden behind a hamburger. It reads anything. Local mbox, local Maildir, remote IMAP; mutt does not care, which is why it works with any provider's storage. It sends through anything. A local mail server, its own SMTP client, or your provider's submission port — same interface, three backends. It is composable with the rest of the terminal: mutt + w3m for HTML, notmuch for corpus-scale search, your real editor for composing. $ doas pkg_add mutt # BSD-style package naming # Debian/Ubuntu-style: apt install mutt (neomutt is the fork with extra patches) Note: vanilla mutt and neomutt share the config language; this page exists in both worlds and every line below opens in both. Where a feature is fork-only, the page says so — and those are extras, not the road. 02 First mail, first keys Start mutt against something real. If you have mail lying in a local Maildir already: $ mutt -f ~/Mail/INBOX # open a specific mailbox $ mutt -y # open the mailbox browser (see section 04) And the first keyboard vocabulary — small, and it never changes: Key Moves j / k (and arrows) Down / up through messages or entries. <Enter> Open the message (pager view). q Close current view (pager → index; index → quit). c Change mailbox (see = and ? expansion below). d / u Mark deleted / undelete (a D in the index; real purge at exit). s Save message to a mailbox (copy+delete in one move). r / g / L Reply / group (all) reply / list reply. v View attachments of the message. ? Show the whole key map in this context. Use it; it is a manual living inside the program. Note: in mailbox-name prompts, = expands to your folder value ( =Sent is ~/Mail/Sent ) and ! is your spoolfile . That shorthand is why config lines below look so short. 03 The configuration files mutt reads, in order: /etc/Muttrc (or /etc/muttrc ) — the system-wide base; you rarely touch it. ~/.muttrc (or ~/.config/mutt/muttrc ) — everything of yours lives here. Any other file you source from those two — and that is where multi-account life (section 05) comes from. The nothing-to-something core, six lines, no account yet: # ~/.muttrc — the spine set mbox_type = Maildir # maildir > mbox: one file per message set folder = ~/Mail # the root all =names expand into set spoolfile = =INBOX # the default mailbox mutt opens set record = =Sent # copies of what you send set postponed = =Drafts # where postponed drafts live And create the Maildir directories on disk (a shell line, not a mutt line): $ mkdir -p ~/Mail/INBOX ~/Mail/Sent ~/Mail/Drafts ~/Mail/Archive Note: to check your own bindings at any time: ? in the compose screen shows that context's key map, and :set ?postponed echoes the value of a variable. Between those two answers, no config question stays unanswered while mutt is open. Warn: do not copy a stranger's 900-line muttrc before you have your own six lines working. Borrowed configs are how people end up mutt users with no idea why mail moves. Grow yours sideways (sections 04–09), one block at a time. 04 One box, many mailboxes The multi-email box starts with a declaration: which mailboxes exist and which show in the browser. Then every folder gets its own behaviour: # ~/.muttrc — declare the landscape mailboxes =INBOX =Sent =Drafts =Archive mailboxes =lists/mutt # lists live in a subtree, declared like the rest # behaviour per folder folder-hook . "set sort=threads" # everywhere: threads folder-hook =lists.* "set sort=date-received" # lists: pure chronology Note the honest limit: mutt does not create folders for you on disk; the mkdir from section 03 done once is why =INBOX resolves. The browser mutt -y opens a list of every mailboxes line with unread counts. Move with j / k , open with Enter ; same keys as everywhere. New folders? Add one mailboxes line; the browser follows. Note: Maildir folders are directories of files, so you can point any plaintext tool at them while mutt has them open. That property is the quiet superpower of the storage format (and the reason mbox gets dropped by everyone who survives a crash once). 05 Many accounts, one muttrc The multi-account pattern is one account-hook (fires when the account is selected) plus per-account files laid out like documents, sourced by the spine: # ~/.muttrc — the hub account-hook $fastmail "source ~/.mutt/fastmail.conf" account-hook $workmail "source ~/.mutt/work.conf" folder-hook fastmail.com.* "source ~/.mutt/fastmail.hooks" folder-hook work.example.com.* "source ~/.mutt/work.hooks" mailboxes ! "imaps://imap.fastmail.com/INBOX" "imaps://imap.work.example.com/INBOX" Each account file carries its own identity, server pair and signature, and declares its own set lines — a mini-section-03, plus the network pair of sections 06–07: # ~/.mutt/fastmail.conf — account template set from = "you@fastmail.com" set realname = "Your Name" set imap_user = "you@fastmail.com" set imap_pass = "" empty = prompt; see the gpg line below set folder = "imaps://imap.fastmail.com/" set smtp_url = "smtps://you@fastmail.com@mail.messagingengine.com" set signature = "~/.mutt/signature.fm" # secrets, decrypted at machine startup — never committed anywhere source "gpg -q --for-your-eyes-only --no-tty -d ~/.mutt/fastmail.gpg |" Warn: account-hook fires on operations (opening a folder, sending), not at startup. If both accounts share secrets in plain set lines, the last file sourced wins at the worst moment. The fix is discipline: per-account files, sourced by hook, never by the spine directly. Where do passwords belong? Not in the file you keep in git. Either way, one thing stays out of the muttrc you keep in git: the password. The classic is a gpg-decrypt-in-flight source "gpg -d ~/.mutt/secrets.gpg |" line that sets imap_pass and smtp_pass at startup; otherwise mutt will simply prompt you, per account, per session.. 06 IMAP: reading from a distance Point folder at an imap(s):// URL and mutt becomes an IMAP client: the mailbox browser lists folders straight off the server, and = names still expand against it. # ~/.muttrc — IMAP core set imap_user = "you@example.com" set imap_pass = "" # empty = prompt; or sourced from gpg set folder = "imaps://imap.example.com/" mailboxes =INBOX "imaps://imap.example.com/OtherFolder" The server-politeness knobs, safe as written: set imap_check_subscribed = yes # trust the server's folder list set mail_check = 60 # imap poll interval, seconds set imap_peek = yes # do NOT auto-mark as read on list set imap_keepalive = 300 # keep NAT/freewalls open during long reads Note: first connect to a new server prints a certificate prompt — read it (fingerprints are the whole point of TLS), accept once, and it is cached. If your provider's certificate chain is normal, this is a once-per-machine moment. 07 SMTP: sending without fear mutt can hand finished mail to your provider directly, skipping any local MTA: # ~/.muttrc — direct submission set smtp_url = "smtps://you@example.com@mail.example.com:465" set smtp_pass = "" # prompt or gpg, like imap_pass set from = "You <you@example.com>" unset write_bcc # do not leak Bcc to the wire; server handles it smtps:// = implicit TLS on port 465 . smtp://...:587 = STARTTLS on the submission port. Prefer smtps when a provider offers both; both are fine. If smtp_url is unset, mutt falls back to the local sendmail -compatible binary — and that is the second, classic route: # ~/.muttrc — delegate delivery to msmtp (config lives in ~/.msmtprc) set sendmail = "/usr/bin/msmtp" Note: pick one route per account and leave the other unset. When both are configured, debugging "why did this mail take the weird path" becomes a zebra hunt. The direct smtp_url route is the one this page recommends for laptops; the sendmail route belongs on the server that already has an MTA. 08 Providers, Gmail included Provider recipes are thin layers over what sections 06–07 already taught. Three common ones: Provider IMAP folder SMTP KVR (ligatório read) Gmail imaps://imap.gmail.com/INBOX smtps://smtp.gmail.com:465 Gmail wraps IMAP in labels; special folders are literally [Gmail]/ -prefixed. Fastmail imaps://imap.fastmail.com/ smtps://mail.messagingengine.com Plain IMAP service; server-side Sent tracked by your record . Any ISP / work server imaps://imap.example.com/INBOX smtps://mail.example.com Same three lines; differences are only the values and the names server-side. Gmail, the whole truth # ~/.mutt/gmail.conf set from = "you@gmail.com" set imap_user = "you@gmail.com" set folder = "imaps://imap.gmail.com/" set spoolfile = "imaps://imap.gmail.com/INBOX" set record = "imaps://imap.gmail.com/[Gmail]/Sent Mail" set trash = "imaps://imap.gmail.com/[Gmail]/Trash" set smtp_url = "smtps://you@gmail.com@smtp.gmail.com:465" set imap_check_subscribed = yes set imap_list_subscribed = yes And the three truths of the label reality (because Gmail is IMAP-wrapped, not native IMAP): Labels are not folders. A message lives in [Gmail]/All Mail and may also appear under any label. mutt browses labels as if they were folders, but deleting manipulates labels, not atoms. Delete means archive or trash — your choice. With trash set above, plain d respects the Trash. For real archive behaviour add a macro that saves to [Gmail]/Archive instead. Decide once; both are one line. Sent lives server-side. Gmail's web UI auto-files every send; point your record at [Gmail]/Sent Mail and both worlds will agree by pointing at the same place. Authentication is its own paragraph, because Gmail is the most common wall: normal password login requires an app password when 2FA is enabled (it should be). The app password is generated in the provider's security settings and behaves like a normal password string, which makes it a perfect fit for the gpg-sourced file from section 05. Warn: do not keep 2FA-disabled mail accounts "just for mutt" no matter how convenient; the app password path is the supported one. Also note that a bare mutt without IMAP+SMTP support compiled in (check mutt -v ) cannot talk to any provider here — your package choice matters. Warn: do not ever keep 2FA-disabled Gmail accounts "just for mutt". The app password path is the supported one; a 2FA-less account is a weaker target, and your inbox is the key to every other account you own. 09 Colors like a command line deserves mutt colors objects , not widgets: bundles such as normal , hdrdefault , quoted , signature , indicator , index . Syntax: color OBJECT foreground background [pattern] , with default meaning "terminal's own". # ~/.muttrc — a complete, calm, dark start color normal white default color hdrdefault cyan default color quoted green default color quoted1 brightgreen default color signature blue default color attachment yellow default color search black brightyellow color indicator black brightgreen color status white blue color tilde brightwhite default color tree magenta default color error red default color message white green color markers red default All of those, as they would land on your dark terminal (CSS speaking for the terminal palette): normal hdrdefault quoted signature attachment indicator status error And the two object+pattern powers that separate a scheme from decoration: # unread messages scream softly color index brightwhite default "~N" # your own outgoing mail, dimmed color index blue default "~P!~F" Note: 256-color identifiers also work ( color normal color252 default ); default keeps the terminal's own. Test choices by eye, live, with :color ... typed straight into the pager — no reload ritual required: it is what resource files wish they were. 10 Patterns: the search superpower l (limit) collapses the index to a sub-world;Everything else — color, hook, save, archive — reuses the same small grammar: Pattern Means Example limit ~N new/unread l ~N → only what waits for you ~f user@host from l ~f butter@club.tld ~t user@host to (you included) l ~t me@tld ~s words subject contains l ~s "invoice" ~F / ~D flagged / deleted l ~F !pattern negation — "does not match" l !~s "cron" & , | , (...) Boolean and / or / grouping l (~N & ~f boss@work.tld) Where it earns with interest: color index ... pattern — the colors in section 09 are pattern-driven. T (tag-pattern) + ; (apply next command to tagged) turns inbox-zero into arithmetic, not patience: one pattern, everything matching, one key, ruined in bulk or filed in bulk. The same notation is mutt's single search language; there is no second one to learn for hooks, colors, limits and tags — which is rare and lovely. Note: the full grammar lives in muttrc(5) , under "Patterns". Keep that man page handy; it is the accidental second manual for the whole program. 11 Keys and macros worth stealing mutt has bind (one key, one named function) and macro (one key, a symphony of virtual keypresses). The handful worth more than their line-count: # ~/.muttrc — quality of life (mutt 1.11+ has the sidebar built in) set sidebar_visible = yes set sidebar_width = 24 # b toggles the sidebar in both index and pager macro index,pager b "<enter-command>set sidebar_visible=!sidebar_visible<enter>" # Tab jumps to the next mailbox with unseen mail bind index \Ct <sidebar-next> # one key to archive: save to =Archive, mark deleted in place macro index,pager a "<save-message>=Archive<enter><delete-message>" # G runs fetchmail-style helpers, if you have one; delete the line if you do not macro index G "<shell-escape>fetchmail</shell-escape><refresh>" Note: the purpose of the macros above is to teach the shape: macro context keys "actions" , actions as if typed in the interface wrapped in <...> function names. Start by simulating your last three manual actions; that is the macro list you actually need, custom-made by your own hands. Warn: two macro-writers' hazards: what genuinely bites is shadowing a default key you use without remembering (bind b away and mutt will never warn), and a macro that fires the wrong context because you forgot the index,pager prefix. When odd behaviour appears, suspect your binds before the program's soul. 12 Hero vocabulary The command-line flags and one-liners that finish the road: Spell What it does mutt -y Mailbox browser — the launcher for your whole declared world. mutt -f =Archive/2026/oct Open one specific mailbox straight away. mutt -F ~/.mutt/minimal Alternate config entirely — the clean-room test for debugging your own muttrc. mutt -n Skip the system-wide config; isolate user settings only. mutt -R Read-only open; inspect an archive with zero risk of touching it. mutt -p Resume the postponed draft (or bind your own key). mutt -s "subject" -a f1.pdf -- dest@host Send from the shell; the classic receipts-and-scripts companion. mutt -H draft.txt Send a pre-written draft file — cron and templating fuel. mutt -e "set editor=vi" One-shot config override, like -xrm in xterm. mutt -v Version + features, incl. IMAP/SMTP support; check before cursing a missing compile. Note: the man pages that finish a hero: mutt(1) (flags), muttrc(5) (every variable and every pattern), and the project's own manual page online if you want the full tutorial voice. Between these sections and those, you are set. Note: and the meta-skill this whole page built: mutt rewards dictating the exact two lines that fix today's annoyance, then stopping. Hoarding muttrc folklore is the fastest route to forgetting why anything works. 13 Your mail, day by day Progress below is stored in this browser ( localStorage ) only. 0 / 12 RESET mutt installed; mutt -v shows IMAP + SMTP support Navigated with only j / k / Enter / q for a full day Six-line spine in ~/.muttrc working (mbox_type, folder, spoolfile, record, postponed) mutt -y opens your declared mailboxes with unread counts At least one honest folder-hook live (sort, colours or both) Reading over IMAP: folder pointed at imaps:// and mail arrives Sending over SMTP ( smtp_url ) or via sendmail /msmtp — one route chosen Passwords sourced from gpg (or prompted) — zero secrets in the muttrc file Two accounts live side by side via account-hook + per-account files Gmail: labels browsed, Trash/Sent configured, app password in use Dark scheme applied by objects; ~N unread line louder than the rest Limited an inbox with l ~N and friends; macros define your archive one-key

Reload the page. 01 Level 01 · Foundations Packets, frames, and the quiet violence of a duplex mismatch What actually happens between typing a URL and seeing a page — and why “the network” is a stack of promises, each one breakable. Gate 1 6 questions ~50 min 1.1 What a network is A network is a group of devices that have agreed on how to encode bits on a medium , how to identify each other , and how to decide who speaks next . That is the whole trick. Every protocol in this manual is a formal answer to one of those three problems, plus the policy layer humans add on top: who is allowed to talk to whom. Two laptops on a desk with one cable between them are a network. So is a data centre with 40,000 servers. The difference is scale, and scale forces hierarchy: you cannot have 40,000 devices all hearing every message, so you introduce addressing, segmentation, and routing. Routing is how a network grows beyond what one device can remember. Mental model Think of a parcel. The street address is the IP address: it describes a location in a hierarchy that routers understand. The name on the door is the MAC address: it identifies the specific network card on the local segment. The courier’s route plan is the routing table. The packing slip is the transport header. If any one of those is wrong, the parcel does not arrive — and the tracking information lies to you in a different way each time. There are two big families of delivery you need to keep separate in your head: Connection-oriented (TCP): a phone call. You establish it, you acknowledge what you hear, you retransmit what was lost, you close it. Reliability has a cost: state, memory, and delay. Connectionless (UDP, IP itself): a postcard. Fire and forget. Cheaper and faster; the application decides whether loss matters. DNS queries, voice, and video generally prefer this. 1.2 Layers and encapsulation The OSI model is a teaching taxonomy with seven layers; the TCP/IP model is what the Internet actually implements, usually drawn with four or five. Neither is physics. Their value is diagnostic: when something breaks, layers tell you which question to ask next and stop you from “rebooting the firewall” because a cable is unplugged. Figure 1-1 · OSI layers mapped to real protocols, devices, and troubleshooting questions # Layer PDU Protocols / addresses Typical device Question it answers 7 Application Data HTTP, DNS, SMTP, SSH Server, proxy What does the user want? 6 Presentation Data TLS, JSON, ASN.1, encoding — How is it represented? 5 Session Data SMB sessions, RPC, TLS session — Who is still talking? 4 Transport Segment (TCP) / Datagram (UDP) TCP, UDP, ports Firewall (L4) Which application, and did it arrive? 3 Network Packet IPv4, IPv6, ICMP, OSPF, BGP Router, L3 switch Where does it need to go? 2 Data link Frame Ethernet, 802.1Q, ARP, PPP Switch, NIC, AP Who on this local link gets it? 1 Physical Bits / symbols 1000BASE-T, 10GBASE-SR, Wi-Fi RF Cable, SFP, antenna Can a signal get there at all? Encapsulation is the nested-envelope effect. Each layer adds a header (and sometimes a trailer) and hands the whole thing down. The receiving side strips them in reverse. The key consequence: a router normally cares only down to Layer 3, and a switch only down to Layer 2 . Each one rewrites a different envelope. Figure 1-2 · One HTTP GET, wrapped four times HTTP GET /index.html · Host: example.com TCP src 51544 → dst 80 · seq, ack, flags, window IPv4 src 192.168.10.10 → dst 93.184.216.34 · TTL 64, proto 6 Ethernet II dst MAC = gateway · src MAC = NIC · type 0x0800 · FCS Bits 1000BASE-T symbols on twisted pair Notice the split-brain in that diagram: the IP addresses are end to end , but the MAC addresses are hop to hop . The source host puts the gateway’s MAC on the frame, not the server’s. Every router along the path strips the old frame and builds a new one. This single fact explains a huge fraction of beginner confusion about ARP, proxy ARP, and NAT. 1.3 The life of one page load Concrete example. A laptop has 192.168.10.10/24 , default gateway 192.168.10.1 , DNS 192.168.10.53 . The user types https://example.com . The server’s address is 93.184.216.34 (a real address historically used by example.com; documentation ranges are used elsewhere in this manual). Figure 1-3 · What happens before the first byte of HTML exists Step Action Protocol / layer What can go wrong here 1 Is the destination local? Compare 93.184.216.34 with the /24 mask → not local, use gateway. L3 logic Wrong mask, wrong gateway, duplicate IP 2 Need gateway’s MAC. ARP broadcast: “Who has 192.168.10.1?” Reply: 00:1a:2b:3c:4d:5e . ARP / L2 ARP blocked, spoofed, or stale; wrong VLAN 3 DNS query for example.com to 192.168.10.53 (UDP/53). DNS / L7 Wrong DNS, blocked UDP/53, captive portal 4 TCP SYN to 93.184.216.34:443, SYN-ACK back, ACK. One RTT consumed. If DNS does not resolve but ping 93.184.216.34 works, it is DNS. This is why the layer model is not academic decoration: it is a binary search over the stack . Note what was proven and what was not. DNS and TCP/443 work. TLS, HTTP, authentication, or the application could still be broken. “Ping works” proves even less — ICMP may be permitted while the application port is blocked, and blocking ICMP does not mean the host is down. 1.4 Ethernet, media, and MTU Ethernet is a family of Layer 1 and Layer 2 standards, not a single cable. The frame format you meet most often is Ethernet II: Figure 1-4 · Ethernet II frame — 64 bytes minimum, 1518 bytes maximum without VLAN tag Field Bytes Purpose Preamble + SFD 7 + 1 Clock synchronisation; not counted in frame size Destination MAC 6 Unicast, broadcast (ff:ff:ff:ff:ff:ff), or multicast Source MAC 6 The transmitting NIC EtherType 2 0x0800 IPv4, 0x86DD IPv6, 0x8100 802.1Q tag, 0x0806 ARP Payload 46–1500 The encapsulated packet, padded if smaller than 46 FCS 4 CRC-32. Bad FCS → frame dropped silently The MTU is the largest payload an interface will send: 1500 bytes on standard Ethernet. That 1500 includes the IP header, so a TCP segment typically carries 1460 bytes of application data (1500 − 20 IP − 20 TCP) before options. A VLAN tag adds 4 bytes, so a tagged frame can be 1522 bytes on the wire while the IP MTU stays 1500. Jumbo frames (9000) exist in storage and data-centre fabrics but must be configured consistently end to end; one 1500-byte hop in the path silently breaks them. Classic outage Path MTU discovery relies on ICMP “fragmentation needed” (Type 3, Code 4). A firewall that blocks all ICMP creates an MTU black hole : small requests work, large responses hang forever. The symptom is famous — a website loads halfway, SSH connects and then freezes after login, VPN tunnels establish but no data passes. Fix the ICMP policy, or clamp TCP MSS on the tunnel, rather than lowering MTU on random hosts. Copper twisted pair (Cat5e, Cat6, Cat6a) is cheap and limited to about 100 m for standard Ethernet. What matters operationally: the optic must match the fibre, the wavelength, and the reach . A 10GBASE-LR optic will not light up over multimode patch leads, no matter how confident the installer is. Duplex is the other silent killer. Full duplex means both sides can transmit simultaneously; half duplex means one at a time. Modern switched Ethernet is full duplex everywhere, and gigabit requires autonegotiation for duplex. When one side is hard-coded full and the other auto-negotiates, the auto side falls back to half — a duplex mismatch . The full-duplex side transmits whenever it wants; the half-duplex side detects “collisions” that are really the other side talking. Result: late collisions, CRC/FCS errors, terrible throughput, and a link that reports “up”. The fix is boring: set both ends to speed auto / duplex auto , or hard-code both to the same values. Never hard-code one end only. And note that late collisions on a link that is supposed to be full duplex is not a cable problem — it is a configuration problem. 1.5 MAC addresses and ARP A MAC address is 48 bits, written as six hex octets. The first three bytes are the OUI (vendor), the last three are assigned by the vendor. The least significant bit of the first octet distinguishes unicast from multicast; the second-least significant bit marks a locally administered address (common in virtual machines and privacy features). Broadcast is all ones: ff:ff:ff:ff:ff:ff . ARP (Address Resolution Protocol, RFC 826 ) glues IPv4 to Ethernet. A host that needs to send to 192.168.10.1 on its own subnet broadcasts “Who has 192.168.10.1? Tell 192.168.10.10”, and the owner replies with its MAC. The result is cached for a few minutes. For a destination off the subnet, the host ARPs for the gateway , then puts the gateway’s MAC on the frame with the server’s IP inside. ARP has no authentication . Any host can answer “that IP is me” and begin receiving traffic meant for the gateway. That is ARP spoofing, and it is the foundation of most on-path attacks in a flat LAN. Level 05 covers the defences (Dynamic ARP Inspection, DHCP snooping, port security, segmentation). For now, remember the design flaw: the protocol trusts whoever speaks first . IPv6 does not use ARP. Neighbor Discovery (ND, RFC 4861 ) uses ICMPv6 Neighbor Solicitation and Advertisement, with Duplicate Address Detection built in. It is still unauthenticated by default; SEND (RFC 3971) exists but is rarely deployed, so ND spoofing is just as real. 1.6 What a switch really does A switch is a Layer 2 bridge with many ports. It learns source MAC addresses into a CAM table (content-addressable memory), then forwards frames destined to a known MAC only out that port. Unknown destination, broadcast, and multicast frames are flooded to all ports in the same VLAN. That is the whole algorithm, and almost every Layer 2 mystery is a consequence of it. Learn — source MAC plus ingress port goes into the table, with an ageing timer (300 seconds by default on Cisco). Forward — destination MAC is known and not on the ingress port: send only there. Flood — destination is unknown, broadcast, or multicast: send everywhere in the VLAN except the source port. A switch gives each port its own collision domain. A broadcast domain is the set of devices that receive each other’s broadcast frames; by default, one VLAN equals one broadcast domain. A router (or a Layer 3 interface) is the boundary between broadcast domains. If you remember only one sentence about switches: they extend broadcast domains and break collision domains . noTime: I like the idea of Eternity Does anyone like the same? :) My posts in this blog have no Time of publication. The posts exist as they were already here, while they continue growing. They have no time reference to me, or to you. Is the perfect static representation of Eternity No Time Reference of Creation Naturally you can investigate this site main page and you will know the date. If that is important to you. :) Why remove the date A date tells the reader how to feel before the first sentence. An article from 2019 is read as old, an article from last week is read as news, and the same words change meaning depending on a number printed above them. I did not want the number to do that work. Without it, the text has to defend itself. Either the reasoning is still valid or it is not, and that judgement belongs to the reader instead of the calendar. What changes Ideas are not published once and finished. A page about documentation gains a paragraph after a new distribution is tested. A page about attacks gains an example after a new scanner appears. If the date stayed at the top, every edit would be invisible and the article would look frozen at the moment of birth, which is exactly the opposite of what happens. So the page grows, and the reader who returns finds a different text in the same address. That is closer to a garden than to a newspaper. The other side of eternity I am not hiding the history. The site is a git repository, and the repository remembers everything: who changed what, when, and with which message. The date exists; it is just not the first thing you see. Eternity here means that the text is never late. Somebody can read it in ten years and find the same argument, still standing or still missing the same thing, without a timestamp telling him that it is too old to matter.

nodeSecurity: Node.js Paranoid Security on Debian: Own The Server, Expose Nothing Mindset: you own the server, so you distrust everything else — code, packages, users, bots, even yourself at 2am. Application below: a tiny secure notes API ( Node.js + Express ) behind Nginx on Debian 12 . Every tip is obsessive on purpose. If it feels excessive, good — attackers are excessive. 0 — The App We Harden (So Tips Have Teeth) Stack: Node.js 20 LTS ( nodejs.org ), Express 4 ( expressjs.com ), PostgreSQL 15 ( postgresql.org ) or SQLite for tiny, Nginx ( nginx.org ) reverse proxy, PM2 or systemd ( pm2 ), Debian 12 Bookworm ( debian.org ), UFW/nftables ( Debian nftables ), Fail2ban ( fail2ban.org ), Certbot ( certbot.eff.org ). PARANOID RULE #1: never commit .env . Ever. .env in git = public secret. Add to .gitignore day zero, rotate any key that touched git history with Gitleaks . node --version # v20.x project/ server.js routes/ middleware/ .env (600, root:www-data? NO — app user only) .gitignore -> .env, node_modules, *.log, *.pem 1 — Debian Base: Minimal, Updated, Boring (Boring = Safe) Install minimal Debian, no desktop. Create deploy user, kill root SSH. Tip in spirit: if you don't need it, uninstall it. apt update && apt full-upgrade -y apt install -y unattended-upgrades apt-listchanges sudo ufw fail2ban unattended-upgrades useradd -m -s /bin/bash deploy usermod -aG sudo deploy # /etc/ssh/sshd_config: PermitRootLogin no, PasswordAuthentication no, AllowUsers deploy systemctl restart ssh ufw default deny incoming; ufw default allow outgoing ufw allow 22/tcp; ufw allow 80/tcp; ufw allow 443/tcp; ufw enable # auto security updates: dpkg-reconfigure -plow unattended-upgrades ✔ Enable unattended-upgrades for security only. Full auto-upgrade can break Node; security-only + weekly manual apt full-upgrade in maintenance window. Links: Debian UnattendedUpgrades , Debian SSH , Debian Security . 2 — .env & Secrets: The Crown Jewels (Treat Like Nuclear Codes) PARANOID RULE #2: .env lives once, on server, chmod 600, owned by app user. No backups to Dropbox. No Slack pastes. No console.log(process.env) . # /opt/notesapp/.env — chmod 600, chown notesapp:notesapp PORT=127.0.0.1:3000 DATABASE_URL=postgres://notesapp:'S0mething-Long-32chars'@127.0.0.1:5432/notes SESSION_SECRET=$(openssl rand -hex 32) # load with dotenv ONLY in dev; in prod use systemd EnvironmentFile npm i dotenv # https://www.npmjs.com/package/dotenv Better than .env on your own server: systemd EnvironmentFile=/etc/notesapp/env (600 root, read at start, never in repo), or HashiCorp Vault ( vaultproject.io ) / SOPS ( mozilla/sops ) for rotation. Validate at boot with dotenv-safe or Zod — crash if SESSION_SECRET < 32 chars . ✔ Scan repo pre-commit with Gitleaks + git-secrets . Add .env.example with fake values only. 3 — Node App Hardening: Headers, Limits, Injection-Proof npm i express helmet cors express-rate-limit express-mongo-sanitize xss-clean hpp cookie-parser csurf jsonwebtoken bcrypt pg zod # https://www.npmjs.com/package/helmet — sets 11+ secure headers // server.js — paranoid skeleton const helmet = require('helmet'); app.disable('x-powered-by'); app.use(helmet({ contentSecurityPolicy: { directives: { defaultSrc: ["'self'"] } }, hsts: { maxAge: 31536000, includeSubDomains: true, preload: true } })); app.use(express.json({ limit: '10kb' })); // no 10MB JSON bombs const limiter = require('express-rate-limit')({ windowMs: 15*60*1000, max: 100, standardHeaders: true }); app.use('/api/', limiter); // auth: bcrypt cost 12, jwt 15min + refresh rotate, httpOnly SameSite=Strict Secure cookies // validate every input with zod; parameterize SQL (pg $1); no string concat PARANOID RULE #3: trust no input — not body, query, header, file, webhook. OWASP NodeJS Cheat Sheet is bedtime reading. Deps: npm audit; npm audit fix , automate with Grype / Snyk / Dependabot . Pin with package-lock.json , npm ci --omit=dev in prod. Never npm install as root. 4 — Run As Nobody: systemd, Non-Root, Read-Only Where Possible # /etc/systemd/system/notesapp.service [Service] User=notesapp Group=notesapp WorkingDirectory=/opt/notesapp EnvironmentFile=/etc/notesapp/env ExecStart=/usr/bin/node /opt/notesapp/server.js Restart=always NoNewPrivileges=true PrivateTmp=true ProtectSystem=strict ProtectHome=true ReadWritePaths=/opt/notesapp/logs AmbientCapabilities= # UMask=0077 so logs 600 ✔ App binds 127.0.0.1:3000 only. World talks to Nginx , never Node directly. ss -tlnp must show Node on localhost. 5 — Nginx Shield: TLS, No Leaks, No .env Ever Served Nginx docs , Mozilla SSL config . server { listen 443 ssl http2; server_name api.example.com; ssl_certificate /etc/letsencrypt/live/api.example.com/fullchain.pem; ssl_certificate_key /etc/letsencrypt/live/api.example.com/privkey.pem; add_header X-Content-Type-Options nosniff always; add_header X-Frame-Options DENY always; add_header Referrer-Policy no-referrer always; client_max_body_size 1m; location / { proxy_pass http://127.0.0.1:3000; proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-For $remote_addr; } location ~ /\. { deny all; } # block .env, .git location ~* \.(env|pem|key|sql|bak)$ { deny all; } } # certbot --nginx -d api.example.com (https://certbot.eff.org/) # test: curl -I https://api.example.com/.env must be 403/404, never 200 PARANOID RULE #4: static root never contains code. root /var/www/public holds only built assets. .git never deployed — deploy tarball via rsync --exclude='.git --exclude=.env' . 6 — Data: Postgres Locked Down, Backups Encrypted # Postgres listens localhost only, scram-sha-256, least privilege: # /etc/postgresql/15/main/postgresql.conf: listen_addresses='127.0.0.1' # pg_hba.conf: host notes notesapp 127.0.0.1/32 scram-sha-256 CREATE USER notesapp WITH PASSWORD 'long-random'; CREATE DATABASE notes OWNER notesapp; REVOKE ALL ON DATABASE notes FROM PUBLIC; # backups: pg_dump | gpg --encrypt | restic to offsite (https://restic.net/) Encrypt backups with GnuPG , store keys offline. Test restore quarterly. Log with pgaudit for sensitive tables. 7 — Perimeter: Fail2ban, Monitoring, No Phone-Home # fail2ban jail for nginx + ssh (http://www.fail2ban.org/) [nginx-limit-req] enabled=true [sshd] maxretry=3 bantime=1h # logs: journalctl + logrotate, 600 perms, ship to local Loki (https://grafana.com/oss/loki/) — no third-party loggers with secrets # monitor: Uptime Kuma (https://github.com/louislam/uptime-kuma) self-hosted, AIDE (https://aide.github.io/) integrity ✔ Run Lynis audit monthly. Redact secrets from logs: logLevel warn , never log tokens, mask with pino-noir ( pino-noir ). 8 — Deploy Checklist (Copy-Paste Paranoia) ☐ .env 600, not in git, Gitleaks clean ☐ npm ci --omit=dev, npm audit clean ☐ helmet + rate-limit + zod validation + parameterized SQL ☐ systemd non-root + NoNewPrivileges + binds localhost ☐ Nginx TLS + security headers + deny .env/.git ☐ UFW deny-all + Fail2ban + unattended-upgrades ☐ Postgres localhost + scram + encrypted restic backups ☐ curl tests: /.env=403, /api without token=401, big JSON=413 ☐ headers check: securityheaders.com + ssllabs.com/ssltest Verify: securityheaders.com , SSL Labs , OWASP Cheatsheets . Own the server = own the responsibility. Expose app, never secrets. Sleep like logs are quiet.

Parece atraso, parece uma ordem perdida, parece um camião que avaria a caminho da rusga , parece um aviso passado num sussurro. Actos pequenos que, multiplicados, salvaram ruas, famílias e por vezes povoações inteiras. A ordem tinha sido feita para não se questionar. Eles questionaram na mesma. 3. As comunidades lembram os seus nomes décadas depois, enquanto os obedientes caíram no esquecimento. Proteger, e não punir, era o que a insígnia devia significar. 5. oMalEmNomeDoBem: Home Monkey Blog Política, Lei e Justiça O Mal em Nome do Bem Fazer o mal em nome do Bem: como os governos usaram soldados e polícias, durante séculos, sob ordens feitas para não se questionar. 1. O padrão Quase todos os séculos repetem a mesma frase: a causa é o Bem, logo o acto é permitido. Deus, nação, ordem, segurança, revolução, paz. Sob essas palavras, homens comuns queimaram aldeias , torturaram presos, espancaram multidões, deportaram famílias e calaram testemunhas. A desculpa é limpa. O acto é sujo. Esse intervalo é o assunto desta página. Só cumpria ordens foi dito em todas as línguas que alguma vez tiveram um exército ou uma polícia. 2. Ordens feitas para não se questionar Durante séculos, desobedecer foi punido com mais força do que a crueldade. O soldado que recusava podia ser chicoteado, preso ou fuzilado. O polícia que recusava podia perder o salário, a patente e o futuro. O sistema escolheu a obediência . A instrução ensinou o corpo a mover-se antes de a mente perguntar porquê. O segredo escondeu a cadeia completa. O papel transformou a morte em procedimento, transferência, pacificação, limpeza. Questionar era traição. Obedecer era dever. Foi assim que o mal virou rotina. 3. Soldados ao longo da história Cruzadas, guerras coloniais, guerras mundiais, contra-insurreições. Jovens longe de casa, a quem disseram que o inimigo é menos humano, a quem disseram que a ordem vem de cima, a quem disseram que a história vai agradecer. Nem as armas nem a farda apagam isso. Depois veio sempre a mesma frase: fizemos o que nos mandaram. Nuremberga respondeu uma vez, com clareza: cumprir ordens não apaga a responsabilidade. Mesmo assim, os exércitos continuam a ensinar primeiro a obediência e só depois a consciência. 4. Polícias ao longo da história A polícia fez o mesmo mais perto de casa: espancamentos nas celas, detenções falsas, provas plantadas, cargas sobre multidões, protecção paga, silêncio sobre colegas. A ordem aqui raramente é escrita. É um aceno, um código no rádio, uma quota, um «trata disso». Como a polícia escreve o auto , também escreve a história. Resta o discurso e a rua . Por isso todos os dossiês sérios sobre polícia voltam sempre às mesmas exigências: identificação visível, registos escritos, queixas independentes, câmaras que não se podem desligar. 5. Governos e actividade criminosa Grande parte da actividade criminosa da história não foi feita por fora-da-lei. Foi feita por homens assalariados, com carimbos, processos e medalhas: deportações, desaparecimentos forçados, esquadrões da morte, programas de tortura, vigilância em massa, guerras agressivas vendidas como defesa. Guardas prisionais, guardas de fronteira, serviços de informações e milícias privadas usaram a mesma defesa: eu não faço a política, eu aplico-a. 6. Hoje o abuso é menos comum Tribunais, imprensa livre onde ainda existe, telemóveis com câmara e leis de direitos humanos tornaram o abuso aberto mais difícil. Um soldado ou um polícia hoje sabe que alguém pode estar a filmar. Isso importa. Mas a estrutura sobreviveu em formas mais suaves: ataques decididos a partir de ecrãs, recolha massiva de dados, devoluções nas fronteiras, detenção administrativa, castigo automático onde nenhum humano assina a ordem. Menos sangue na rua, a mesma falta de perguntas no gabinete. 7. Como recusar uma ordem criminosa Uma ordem não é um cheque em branco. Pergunta quatro vezes: é legal, é necessária, é proporcional, aceitarias se fosse contra ti. Se falhar, pede por escrito, guarda cópia, conta a alguém fora da cadeia de comando. Nunca entregues a tua consciência a outra pessoa para a guardar. obsdLearning: I figure out that OpenBSD can be my main operating system In case I wish to use this OS as a Firewall, I should try to use it, without installing any extra software, to be sure that my "Router" is secure. But, by reading OpenBSD documentation, I see that is possible to use this OS as a Desktop with Firefox, and many other software that I normally use when using Linux. In fact, I can even emulate a Linux box inside OBSD and run the applications that I like to run that are not in OBSD, to access them with easy. The popularity of this OS is not big, while I am not searching for popularity, but for stability. By default, if you try to use Firefox the system will be damn slow and You may ask: "But why?". The answer is on the default configurations that OBSD runs on. If you change it, you will have a "fast OS" without being damn slow. Is less secure? ( probably is, but if you are not serving any public service, is not a big deal to change those configurations ). So, I start trying to use 'vi' without install 'vim'. Is a bit strange, since there a few changes, but if you know how to play with Vim, then 'vi' will be a bit different but not so much. There is no default browser, therefor, I need to install a minimal package, like 'w3m' or 'elinks', which are my favorite browsers for the terminal. With this in mind, I can configure a machine to be a dedicated firewall, while having others that are not, but Desktops. Sadly, at least for me, I need to have a dedicated machine using Linux, since the Cloudflared application to create a tunnel between my personal server and Cloudflare servers, don't run on OBSD or in FBSD. At that point, I will keep the most accessible Linux OS in the world, which is (in my opinion, Debian). I can run it inside a VM or in a dedicated Machine. For this, I really prefer to dedicate a Machine for this, since I can run all the necessary software, without hacking the system to make it work. When using a Tunnel, all traffic is managed by the service we are using, not by OBSD. The fascinating fact is that, we don't need to open Extra ports to accept connections from the outside world, and we can validate all http requests using Cloudflare API, to be sure that all connections we accept, are from a trusted source. The developers are integrated with awesome projects, that are independent from OBSD main OS. These people care to create a stable and secure OS and with that in mind, I feel safe . I start to read about the default shell they use, which is the Korn Shell , which anyone can find some documentation in the IBM site, while there is another community called SpaceWorks that is a Awesome source of Information and a very nice platform to clear our doubts. In this research on "how to use OBSD" without installing (too much extra software), I am learning a bit more about OBSD flow. For example, I really like to know the difference betweeen folder and files, which I didn't find how to setup colors of the listed files, I can use the (alias ls='ls -F') in the .profile and with that, I can see if the listed files are files or folders. It would be the same if using 'ls -p'. Anyway, I always like to have this sensation that I am upgrading everything I know, with something that give me a new sensation of stability and security. Nothing is unbreakable and nothing is eternal, but this project is made by many users that are very experienced with C, C++, Rust, Go, Python, Perl and many others languages that may be useful to use in any OS. I am still in doubt about what is best (between pure VMMs or Qemu). Because Qemu have better suport for Graphics, using Qemu can have some advanges, even if the main objective is to use a Linux without X. I will continue testing while learning. Read the Source, don't be dependent of my 'bla bla bla'. These notes are made for me, not to help someone else

openbsdCompilation: ↶ Home Field Manual OBC-5 · compilation from source OpenBSD Compilation for Developers Everything in one page: a tree, an obj directory, a kernel, the whole userland, one X, and all the traps that bite between two good builds. Written for people who read source code on purpose. kernel · userland · xenocara · ports · release vanilla JS · CSS3 · no dependencies progress lives in this browser 01 Why compile at all OpenBSD ships binaries and releases every six months, and for most machines sysupgrade is the correct answer. Compiling is the correct answer for other roles: Tracking fixes between releases: -stable exists precisely so you can build today's stability fixes on top of a released base, without moving to -current. -current developers and testers: the snapshot base plus a compiled tree is how the project eats its own food every day. If you compile -current you are implicitly volunteering as the tester. Custom-kernel work: drivers, kernel experiments or a smaller GENERIC for an odd machine. Ports work: the ports(7) system is designed to be driven from source on your own machine, and the maintainers' workflow (patches, make update-patches , bulk builders) assumes it. Building releases: make release produces the install media and the sets you supply to your own machines, the same way the project produces theirs. Note: compiling is not a security upgrade by itself. A random local build of -current is less trustworthy than a signed release. The difference is that you can read every line you run — which is the point. 02 The machine The complete build (kernel + userland + X + ports infrastructure) is not large by modern standards, but it is the sum of many small machines. Plan like this: Resource Minimum Comfortable Notes RAM 2–4 GB 8 GB+ Kernel link time is the memory peak; big ports can spike hard. Disk — source trees ~3 GB 4–5 GB src , xenocara , ports checkouts. Disk — build + product ~15 GB 25–40 GB /usr/obj , /usr/xobj , /usr/lobj , DESTDIR, RELEASEDIR, distfiles, packages. CPU anything “more cores” Base builds are largely serial by design; ports bulk builds parallelise much better. Two filesystem decisions pay for themselves immediately: Give /usr or, better, a dedicated /usr/obj partition room to breathe. Running out of space during make build is the beginner classic. Put the build output on your fastest disposable storage. obj directories exist to be deleted. doas and the shell you will live in Root does the installing; work can stay interactive. Check your privilege tool: $ grep root /etc/doas.conf permit persist :wheel Note: make build shells out and expects sudo -style elevation to work non-interactively. With doas, permit persist for your group is the smooth path; otherwise prefix with SUDO=doas . 03 Get a tree Everything starts from CVS. Pick an anoncvs server near you from the list on the project website, then check out the trees you need: # base source, the one everything else depends on $ cd /usr $ cvs -qd anoncvs@server/pub/OpenBSD-src checkout -P src # X11 sources (Xenocara) $ cvs -qd anoncvs@server/pub/OpenBSD-xenocara checkout -P xenocara # ports for third-party software $ cvs -qd anoncvs@server/pub/OpenBSD-ports checkout -P ports To update a tree later, move it forward instead of checking out over it: $ cd /usr/src $ cvs -q up -Pd Three ways to be slightly wrong Rule one: install the matching snapshot or release first . A -current tree compiled against an old base mixes header generations and behaves in ways that waste your weekend. sysupgrade to the matching snapshot before touching cvs. Note: on -stable, install each <nn>.patch file for your release before building; the patches are the errata with build instructions attached. Note: keep trees for different flavours separate. A -current workstation and a -stable server can live on one disk if their trees are separate, but they must not share obj output. 04 Branches of the same rock One CVS tree, three flavours, and the build steps differ mostly in what you expect from them: Flavour Tag / have Wait for it to be Get updates by -release the install media frozen syspatch only -stable -rstab from the release tag conservative cvs pull + recompile -current unstable HEAD fast-moving cvs pull + recompile + read current.html -stable: born from the release tag with bug fixes back-ported. API-stable enough that a running host keeps its promises across a rebuild. -current: where development happens. Between major ABI changes it will require bootstrapping steps; current.html on the website is the contract, read it before you pull, not after you break. Never mix a -current kernel with a -stable userland, or the other way. The libc/kernel ABI pair moves together. 05 Order of operations Source build is a dance with a fixed order. Skipping a step produces the famous “file not found but everything looks fine” classes of failure: 1 Snapshot or release base in place sysupgrade / syspatch first. The tree must match the day's base. 2 make obj Symlink mirrors for every object directory into /usr/obj , so binaries never pollute the source tree itself. 3 Kernel Either the whole make kernel or a configured variant. A KARL-linked kernel comes from the release machinery; a hand-built one gets you to work. 4 Includes and userland make includes (or a straight make build , which does it in order) puts fresh headers into /usr/include before anything else is compiled against them. 5 Xenocara Same idea, /usr/lobj + /usr/xobj , installed over the old X. 6 Ports / release Your target ports, or a whole make release run if you are producing install sets. Note: make obj is re-runnable and idempotent. When in doubt, rm -rf /usr/obj/* and run it again. It takes seconds; debugging a mixed build takes evenings. 06 Build the kernel The plain path that follows the source tree as written: # from a clean tree with objects made $ cd /usr/src $ make obj $ make kernel # builds every kernel flavor for your arch from the shared obj area Installing it by hand make kernel puts the result under /usr/obj/... . Move it into place and keep the old one bootable — the boot loader understands > -prefixed names like boot> boot #bsd.prev : $ doas cp /usr/obj/sys/arch/$(machine -i)/compile/GENERIC/bsd /bsd $ doas rm -f /obsd && doas ln /bsd /obsd $ doas reboot A custom kernel Copy the stock config out of the way, edit it, and build the same way the tree does: $ cd /usr/src/sys/arch/$(machine -i)/conf $ cp GENERIC.MP KLUDGE $ vi KLUDGE # keep the diff small and boring $ config KLUDGE $ cd ../compile/KLUDGE $ make clean && make Warn: do not blind-delete devices you actually use, and do not remove wd0* / sd0* -style disk nodes or things your filesystem depends on. A “lean” kernel that cannot read its own disk is a form of modern haiku. Why is my kernel bigger / smaller than the stock one? Options and drivers differ, and KARL (Kernel Address Randomization Link) pads the stock one deliberately. Functionally, a hand-built kernel is fine; release builds do the KARL pass (two links so symbol placement differs between snapshot kernels). If you care about matching the project's randomisation behaviour, build via make release hooks. 07 Build userland This is the long loop: libc , /bin , /usr/bin , daemons, the compiler toolchain. Give it hours, not minutes. $ cd /usr/src $ make obj # idempotent; re-run freely $ make includes # headers before things compiled against them $ doas make build # or: $ SUDO=doas make build What make build will do to your machine, roughly in order: make cleandir -adjacent cleanup of built objects, make includes into /usr/include , the compiler bootstrap dance, every library, binary and manual page for your host, system configuration updates where needed (run sysmerge if told). After it finishes with no errors, reboot into the new world and run sysmerge if prompted — config file differences land outside make's jurisdiction. Warn: interrupting make build is legal ( Ctrl+C ) but restarting requires a clean /usr/obj and a fresh make obj at minimum. The tree does not reliably resume mid-flight, and half-installed binaries hide trickier bugs than missing ones. 08 Build Xenocara X sources follow the same choreography with different directories. The bootstrap target makes the meta-tooling, then the build proceeds: $ cd /usr/xenocara $ make bootstrap $ make obj $ doas make build Object output lands in /usr/xobj , intermediate tools in /usr/lobj . Like the base tree, both are disposable. Note: build userland before X. Xenocara links against freshly built libraries; doing it backwards is one of the rare genuine ordering traps left in the flow. 09 Ports: the source of everything else ports(7) is the third-party build system. Unlike base, it is designed to be driven on your machine, and it has opinions about tarballs, checksums and privilege separation. One port, properly # find it $ cd /usr/ports $ make search key= example # download + checksum (this is what verifies against a known digest) $ cd editors/example $ doas make fetch # build and install; config files ask politely via sysmerge-style dialogs $ doas make install Everyday knobs that keep your tree clean: Knob Does WRKOBJDIR Where work directories are created (keep them off the tree disk). DISTDIR Where source tarballs accumulate (share it across machines). PKG_PATH For prebuilt packages, the counterpoint to ports: pkg_add is what make install compares itself against. FLAVOR Build variants declared by the port ( make show=FLAVORS lists them). Maintainer tooling make update-patches regenerates patches/ from your work/ volunteer edits — the polite way to feed fixes upstream. portcheck / port-lib-depends / make wantlib-args keep the metadata honest. dpb (from ports infrastructure) drives parallel dependency-aware builds — the same engine the bulk builders use. One machine, many cores, correct dependency order for free. Warn: never make install untrusted ports as root on your only machine. Port build code is software you have not read yet, running before you install it. Separate VM or builder account is the security advice both from the project and from this page. 10 Release engineering make release walks the whole tree and produces the install sets your install media consumes: base , comp , xbase , man , and the bsd -family kernels. This is where KARL happens too: the kernel is linked twice so each snapshot gets a different memory layout. $ cd /usr/src $ doas env DESTDIR=/dest RELEASEDIR=/rel make release # then the two extra passes that verify it $ doas env DESTDIR=/dest2 make release 'UPDATE= no' # see FAQ for exact knobs Honest advice: read release(8) before your first run and do the first release in a VM. The knobs (DESTDIR, RELEASEDIR, the check-passes) have changed shape between versions, and your reading of the manual is the only thing guaranteed to match the tree you checked out. Note: ports and xenocara have their own release flows ( dpb for ports packages, make release in xenocara). They compose with the base release but are their own documents. 11 Traps and their traps The failure modes are boringly repetitive. Recognising them by symptom saves an afternoon each: Symptom Usually Fixed by Compiler killed, cc1 OOM Not enough RAM for link time More RAM, or build on a machine with swap. /usr/obj: No space left mid-build Disk arithmetic was optimistic Move obj to a bigger fs; clean other obj dirs. make build fails in weird template files after a partial edit Mixed tree state, stale objects rm -rf /usr/obj/* , make obj , restart clean. Kernel boots, userland refuses to run Kernel/userland age mismatch Match with the same tree and the same base. make -j N breaks the base build Base Makefiles are not parallel Run them serially (ports and dpb parallelise instead). Timestamps confused, make loops forever Clock skew, NFS with bad timesource NTP the build host; local disks built better. The big one: a tree that is halfway between two CVS states is the single most common self-inflicted wound. openbsdDesktop: ↶ Home Field Manual OBS-7 · desktop values that survive OpenBSD for Desktops The default install guards the machine like a server. A desktop needs the same discipline with roomier ceilings — enough that Firefox plays a video while the system keeps answering, without a single change that cannot be undone by deleting one line. sysctl · sndiod · firefox · wsconsctl · apm vanilla JS · CSS3 · no dependencies every knob is reversible 01 The deal The stock values of a fresh install are chosen to protect machines you never look at. That is why a browser can open too many files and fail, or a media pipeline can exhaust the process ceiling while the desktop crawls. The project itself documents this: the values exist so a runaway service eats the “small” quota first. The deal you are signing when you keep reading: Reversibility first. Most of this page is sysctl at runtime. Reboot clears it if you regret it. Persistence is a plain-text line in /etc/sysctl.conf — remove the line, the value is gone. No recompiled kernels, no -current, no patches. Everything here works on the release you already installed, with the packages the mirrors already serve. No fancy filesystems, no exotic schedulers. The default FFS layout stays; the default services stay. A desktop is the place you should be least creative. Firefox does the media work ; the OS only has to stop tripping it. Note: check every number against your own machine ( sysctl -a prints the current ones). The kernel clamps or rejects values outside its range, and it tells you when it does — listen to it, do not fight it. 02 The values that stop the lag This is the section you came for. Three ceilings cover most desktop slowdowns: file descriptors, the process cap, and the thread cap. A browser is many processes each holding many files when video is rolling; the defaults were sized smaller than that. Sysctl Desktop value Default-ish base Why video lagged kern.maxfiles 10240 7022 Each tab/thread keeps sockets, pipes, media descriptors; the cap lands and the browser queues instead of rendering. kern.maxproc 65000 1310 A modern browser spawns processes per tab. Past the cap, new tabs die or the compositor stalls. kern.maxthread 4096 1024 Media decoding is thread-hungry; when threads get refused, video decodes late — which is the “OS lagging” feel. Apply them live, right now, no reboot: $ doas sysctl kern.maxfiles=10240 $ doas sysctl kern.maxproc=65000 $ doas sysctl kern.maxthread=4096 Then open Firefox, play a video, resize the window, switch tabs. The machine should stay smooth because the browser stopped knocking on a closed ceiling. If a value is refused “Invalid argument” or “Permission denied” , the range on your kernel is different — back off, or read options(4) ; do not shave the kernel. What I am not telling you to change: vm.* percentages, buffer cache ratios, kern.maxclusters beyond sanity, scheduler hacks. On a general-purpose laptop those defaults are right, and turning them is how people “tune” a working system into a mysterious one. Seriously, only three sysctls? For video playback without OS lag, yes in the common case: descriptors, processes and threads are what a browser exhausts first. If your case is different, the evidence is readable: systat vmstat during playback shows you whether the machine is swapping (RAM problem → section 06), starving on descriptors (files problem → this section), or neither (then the lag is mismatched driver rendering → section 04). 03 Testing, then keeping The beauty of sysctls: try, keep, or leave with a one-line difference. Runtime first as above; then, to survive reboots, the same key=value pairs go into /etc/sysctl.conf : # /etc/sysctl.conf — one line each, no 'sysctl' keyword kern.maxfiles=10240 kern.maxproc=65000 kern.maxthread=4096 Confirm the boot result once: $ doas reboot $ sysctl kern.maxfiles kern.maxproc kern.maxthread Discipline that keeps this safe for a normal user: Change one thing at a time and use the machine for an hour. If anything feels strange, delete one line from /etc/sysctl.conf , reboot, done. Keep a note (this page's checklist, or a file) of every line you added. Six months from now “the system changed behaviour” will actually be “past-me added a line”. Do not set values you have no reason for. More is not smoother; mis-sized memory pools are just a new way to be slow. 04 Firefox, tamed Firefox from packages is the right Firefox — it is built against the system's libraries and speaks sndio for audio natively: $ doas pkg_add firefox Video playback on OpenBSD decodes in software through the bundled ffmpeg stack; the machine behind sections 02 and 06 is what makes it smooth. There is one optional forward step: Note (optional): on machines whose DRM driver exposes hardware video decode (newer Intel graphics are the usual candidates), Firefox can attempt VAAPI: about:config → media.ffmpeg.vaapi.enabled → true , restart, and check whether videos actually behave. It is per-profile and revertible with the same switch set back to false . If there is no improvement — or video gets worse — flip it back and move on. No loss. Warn: do not chase acceleration through unofficial builds, forks or scripts pasted from forums. A browser that runs outside the package system is un-signed, un-updated and a genuine security regression on the machine you can least afford to regress. Small habits that keep it fast Keep the profile small: hundreds of dormant tabs cost memory on any OS. Let the package system update it ( pkg_add -u ) instead of living between versions. If the browser itself freezes but the desktop answers, that is an in-browser problem — sections 02/06 will not fix a broken profile; a fresh one will. 05 Audio without crackle sndiod is already running and mixing by default. Desktops rarely need tuning; when video + music at once hiss or crackle under load, the device buffer can grow a little: # /etc/rc.conf.local — only if audio crackles under load sndiod_flags=-b2400 $ doas rcctl set sndiod flags -b2400 $ doas rcctl restart sndiod Bigger buffer = more latency (a few milliseconds you will not notice) in exchange for staying fluid when the CPU spikes. Defaults first; change only what crackles. Per-application volume just works on sndio ; per-app mixers from other systems do not exist here and are not missed. Note: if audio devices change (plug/unplug, monitors with speakers), sndiod re-reads devices on the fly. Persistent weirdness is usually the volume knob of the wrong device, not broken config. 06 RAM arithmetic No sysctl rescues too little RAM. Video in a browser is a few gigabytes of anonymous memory; the page daemon starts clawing pages back as soon as the machine is tight, and that reclaiming is the real “OS is lagging” experience — the system keeps running while it swaps your video in and out. $ systat vm 1 # watch pi/po (pages in/out) during a video 8 GB : fine for one browser session + WM + terminal. 16 GB : the comfortable desktop number. How to be honest about it: play your worst case (video + video call + editor) and watch systat vm . If pi/po churn while the system feels mushy, you need more memory, not more tuning. Swap exists to exist, not to be a second RAM: leave the default swap sized at install time, leave the virtual-memory ratios alone, and treat “ vm.anonmin ”-style advice as something for people with a measurement, not a feeling. Note: if the machine is old-slow rather than out-of-memory, upgrade path is RAM → SSD → patient browser habits. The sysctls of section 02 only remove the artificial ceiling. 07 Trackpads and keyboards These are wsconsctl knobs — same reversibility as sysctls. Trackpad tapping and natural scrolling behaviour live here: $ doas wsconsctl -w mouse.tapping=1 # tap = click, live $ doas wsconsctl -w mouse.scrolling=0 # 0 traditional, 1 natural And to keep them after reboot, /etc/wsconsctl.conf takes the bare key=value lines: # /etc/wsconsctl.conf mouse.tapping=1 mouse.scrolling=0 Keyboard layouts follow the same pattern; list what your console understands and set it live with wsconsctl keyboard.map= ... then persist in the same file. Two knobs on the laptop (tapping + scrolling) cover 90% of the “OpenBSD feels unfinished” first impressions. Warn: do not autoload random X11 driver flags or modeline hacks from forums to fix a trackpad. The wsconsctl route is the project's own and it survives xenodm restarts; the forum route survives nothing. 08 Battery, lid, suspend Laptops get the pleasant part of OpenBSD: suspend ( zzz ) works out of the box, and the lid action is a sysctl: $ apm # battery state + performance mode $ doas apm -A # automatic performance adjustment $ doas sysctl machdep.lidaction=1 # close lid = suspend (1); 0 leaves it alone Persist the lid behaviour in /etc/sysctl.conf like the others: # /etc/sysctl.conf machdep.lidaction=1 Allow yourself to suspend without a password being typed each time — acceptable only for zzz itself: # /etc/doas.conf permit nopass :wheel cmd zzz Warn: permit nopass otherwise gets you a root-shaped hole in the name of convenience. One command, exactly that command. Note: after suspend, if the clock is off, ntpd re-syncs automatically. If keys repeat weirdly until the next reboot, that is your machine's firmware being ancient, not OpenBSD's fault alone — the same happens walking between three other OSes. 09 A window manager that answers cwm ships in base and is the truthful answer to “what WM on OpenBSD”. X as a whole is started by xenodm : $ doas rcctl enable xenodm $ doas rcctl start xenodm And your ~/.xsession simply must point at it (this file is the only thing between you and a black screen; keep it tiny): # ~/.xsession . /etc/X11/xinit/xinitrc.d/40-systray 2>/dev/null || true xsetroot -solid \"#070b12\" exec cwm Why cwm and not something showier: it is keyboard-first, memory-flat, updated with the base system, and sports the most honest manual page in any WM. Window managers from packages (fvwm, i3 and so on) also work — if a package install goes wrong, it is removable and you still have twm and a console. Note: keep xenodm enabled rather than starting X from a bare console every time; multiuser discipline survives by accident otherwise. 10 Fonts and the packages worth having A desktop without good fonts is a desktop you describe as “ugly”. This is fixed by packages, and it cannot break anything: $ doas pkg_add noto-fonts noto-fonts-emoji dejavu-fonts fonts: a full family + emoji covers all web pages you will open. audio/video: nothing extra; ffmpeg rides inside Firefox and friends via packages. tools: curl , git , vim (or neovim), zsh — all from packages, all disposable. updates are one command, run occasionally: pkg_add -u . Note: stay on -release / -stable as a normal user. -current is a full-time hobby; a browser that changes under your video every week is a form of self-harm. 11 The boring parts that matter User discipline: live as a normal user; doas for the few things above. Everything on this page runs through doas, never inside a bare root shell. Email noise: the daily maintenance cron mail tells you about things like “disk nearing capacity”. Read it instead of filtering it: it is the OS whispering. /etc/motd : shorten it. Reclaiming screen inches — not “tuning”, but the daily reward. dmesg and sysctl -a : after every change, compare once before/after before calling it “better”. Feelings lie; diffs do not. Back up the small config: these are now “your” files — /etc/sysctl.conf , /etc/wsconsctl.conf , /etc/doas.conf , ~/.xsession . Four files; save a copy with tar when they feel right. Warn: nothing on this page should push you to enable services from rcctl you cannot name the purpose of. A desktop with 8 enabled daemons is a small server wearing a desktop's face, and it inherits a server's attack surface with none of its pay. 12 Cheat sheet Goal Command Un-stick video ceilings (live) doas sysctl kern.maxfiles=10240 kern.maxproc=65000 kern.maxthread=4096 Keep them over reboots same three pairs, one per line, in /etc/sysctl.conf See current values sysctl kern.maxfiles kern.maxproc kern.maxthread Audio breathing room rcctl set sndiod flags -b2400 && rcctl restart sndiod Trackpad manners doas wsconsctl -w mouse.tapping=1 (+ line in /etc/wsconsctl.conf ) Suspend now / on lid doas zzz / machdep.lidaction=1 Watch memory churn systat vm 1 X with cwm rcctl enable xenodm , exec cwm in ~/.xsession Fonts pkg_add noto-fonts noto-fonts-emoji dejavu-fonts Everything fresh pkg_add -u 13 Your desktop, checked off Progress below is stored in this browser ( localStorage ) only — closing the page keeps it. 0 / 10 RESET sysctl -a captured before any change (your before-picture) kern.maxfiles=10240 applied and kept in /etc/sysctl.conf kern.maxproc=65000 applied and kept kern.maxthread=4096 applied and kept Video in Firefox plays smoothly with tabs switching beside it systat vm watched during playback; pi/po calm (or RAM planned) Audio checked under load; -b2400 applied only if it crackled Trackpad tapping/scroll set via wsconsctl and persisted Lid + suspend + doas nopass for zzz only The four config files copied away once ( sysctl.conf , wsconsctl.conf , doas.conf , ~/.xsession )
