ordersAndConscience: Home Monkey Blog · Big Dossier English Português Politics, Law & Justice · Big Dossier Orders and Conscience The same machine, seen from both sides: evil done in the name of the Good, good done in the name of evil — and what the psychology of obedience, moral injury and refusal tells us about the person inside the uniform. Obedience Refusal Moral injury De-escalation Sources Bilingual How to read this dossier You wear a uniform, 15 minutes — read 1 , 2 and 7 . The four questions in section 7 are the part worth memorising. You are a citizen, 20 minutes — read 3 , 4 and 5 . These are the two faces of the same machine, and the bill. You train people, 30 minutes — read 6 , 7 and 8 . Section 8 is the part institutions hate. You have five minutes — section 2 : the answer that the law gave in 1946 and never took back. You want the whole history — read 3 and 4 together, century by century: every order in the first list has a name in the second. 1. How obedience is manufactured No state has ever needed to convince most of its people to be cruel. It only has to arrange the situation so that cruelty looks like procedure. The rest is engineering, and the engineering has been studied for eighty years. The experiments that still explain the office Stanley Milgram's 1963 study at Yale put ordinary volunteers in front of a machine they believed delivered shocks to a stranger. A man in a grey coat said please continue . About sixty-five percent went all the way to the highest switch. When two peers openly refused, obedience collapsed to a small fraction; when the authority left the room, or was replaced by an ordinary man in a shirt, it fell sharply too. The finding was never about Germans, or about evil people: it was about how much the obedience of a normal person depends on the room he is standing in. Solomon Asch showed the same soft machinery with lines of different length: people will deny their own eyes to agree with a group. In the standard experiments about a third of answers followed the majority, and roughly three quarters of participants conformed at least once. Nobody was threatened. Being the only one who disagrees was cost enough. The Stanford prison study of 1971 is still quoted as proof that power corrupts. It should be quoted as a warning about evidence instead: recordings released decades later show coaching, rehearsed lines and a guard role played to please the researcher. The lesson survives, but inverted — a study can be built to produce the result the designer wants, which is exactly what an institution does when it dresses a decision as a policy. The four tools of distance Albert Bandura described moral disengagement as a set of switches that let a person do harm and keep a clean self-image. They appear in every bureaucracy, in every language: Moral justification — the cause is Good, therefore the act is permitted. God, nation, order, security, peace, revolution. Euphemism — pacification, collateral damage, enhanced interrogation, redistribution, cleaning the area. The word arrives before the act and hides it while it happens. Diffusion of responsibility — I do not make policy, I apply it. The signature is one of forty signatures. The order came from above, and above is a committee. Dehumanisation — they are not like us, they are a mob, they are numbers on a list, they are a risk score. A soldier , a police officer and a clerk in an office are trained in the first two and protected by the third. The fourth one is announced on the radio. Nobody starts at the grave Complicity is built in steps small enough to be deniable: deliver the message, keep the file, sign the transfer, do not ask why the list is shorter. Each step makes the next one cheaper, because refusing now would mean admitting what the previous step was. This is why the first refusal is the strongest and the last one is almost impossible. Reserve Police Battalion 101, Józefów, July 1942: the commander offered those who did not feel able to shoot the option of stepping out. Most men still killed. The ones who stepped out were not punished, were not transferred, and were not killed. Refusal was possible — that is the uncomfortable, important fact that the defence "there was no choice" cannot survive. The price of being the one who asks Against the moral cost stands a small, ordinary, human cost: transfer, mockery, no promotion, the locker room going quiet, the feeling of being the problem for the group. Armies and police forces have always known this and have used it as a free enforcement mechanism. Distrust is cheaper than discipline. The counterweights are documented too: visible identification , written records , an independent complaint route, and a chain of command that publicly protects the person who said no. The soft machine Modern obedience rarely arrives as a shout. It arrives as a screen: a risk score, a quota of fines, an automated flag, a list of names, a pushback order written in administrative language. The old sentence survives intact, only the grammar changed: I only followed orders became I only applied the rule . The distance grew from an office wall to an interface, and distance is the ingredient that does the work. 2. What the law already decided The excuse that emptied the twentieth century — Befehl ist Befehl , an order is an order — was answered in writing, with sources that any uniformed person can read in ten minutes. Nuremberg Principle IV (formulated by the UN International Law Commission, 1950): acting under the order of a government or a superior does not relieve a person of responsibility under international law, provided a moral choice was in fact possible to him . That last clause is the whole doctrine. It does not say obey is always criminal; it says obedience is not a shield. Rome Statute, article 33 (1998): superior orders are not a defence when the order is manifestly unlawful — and orders to commit genocide or crimes against humanity are, by definition, manifestly unlawful. Customary international humanitarian law, rule 155 : obeying a superior order does not relieve a subordinate of criminal responsibility if he knew the act was unlawful, or should have known. Conscience is a protected right : article 18 of the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights protects freedom of thought, conscience and religion; the UN human rights system reads conscientious objection to military service as a legitimate exercise of that right. The European Court of Human Rights said it plainly in Bayatyan v. Armenia (2011), after decades in which it had avoided the question. In Portugal , article 41(6) of the Constitution states that the right to conscientious objection is guaranteed in the terms of the law — a sentence written in 1976, two years after a war ended and a regime fell. Two honest qualifications, because a dossier that only sells comfort is useless. The first: the law protects you afterwards, sometimes. On the day, in the corridor, with a supervisor waiting for your answer, the law is not in the room. Only procedure and allies are. Section 7 is therefore about procedure, not principles. The second: "manifestly unlawful" is a higher bar than "unpleasant" or "pointless" or "politically embarrassing". An order you dislike is not an illegal order. The test is narrower than conscience and wider than rank, and it is worth learning precisely because it protects the refuser from becoming merely insubordinate. Never hand your conscience to someone else to hold. 3. Face one — evil in the name of the Good Every century repeats the same sentence: the cause is Good, therefore the act must be permitted. What follows is the file, not the sermon. Figures follow the historians and the commissions of inquiry; where estimates differ, they differ, and the difference is noted. All Before 1900 1900–1945 1945–1990 After 1990 36 / 36 1099 · Jerusalem After the walls of the First Crusade 's prize fell, the population of the city was killed in the name of God. Medieval chroniclers claimed tens of thousands; modern estimates are lower, still in the low thousands. The slaughter was described by the winners as an act of purification. 1209 · Béziers The Albigensian Crusade against the Cathars. The line kill them all, God will know his own is attributed to a papal legate and may be legend — the sack of the city was not. Crusades against Christians, once started, never paused for a theological check. 1478–1834 · Spanish Inquisition An institution built to punish belief, with a bureaucracy, a filing system, an interrogation practice and a public ceremony. Most of the accused were never executed; the machinery that made the threat credible was the point. 1492 · Spain, and 1496 · Portugal Jews expelled from Spain, then forced to convert or leave in Portugal. An administrative decision, taken in law, executed by officials, with the property of the expelled staying behind. 1885–1908 · Congo Free State Leopold II of Belgium ran a private colony as a rubber concession. Hostages were taken to force quotas; hands were cut as proof of ammunition used. Roger Casement's 1904 consular report and E. D. Morel's campaign dragged it into the light. Estimates of population loss run from one million to several million, and the disagreements are about method, not about cruelty. 1904–1908 · German South-West Africa Von Trotha's extermination order against the Herero, then the Nama. Roughly four fifths of the Herero died; the survivors were used as forced labour. Germany formally recognised the killings as genocide in 2021, and agreed to a fund of about €1.1 billion. It took 116 years, and the negotiations were with the government of a country, not with the descendants in the room. 1915 · Armenia Intellectuals arrested on 24 April, then the deportation law of May, then the marches and the killing units. An estimated 1.5 million people, out of the war 's chaos, by design. More than thirty states and the overwhelming majority of historians call it genocide; the denial continues as a state policy, which is itself part of the file. 1917 · Chemin des Dames After a failed French offensive, soldiers refused to attack again. Thousands were involved, hundreds sentenced, dozens executed. They were not traitors: they had concluded that the tactic was slaughter and that obedience was the fuel. 1918 · Kiel German sailors refused an order to sail out for a last battle they could not win. The refusal spread, the republic was declared, the war stopped. A mutiny ended what a war had started. 1932–33 · Ukraine Famine imposed by requisition and administrative orders: an estimated 3.5 to 5 million dead. It has been recognised as a genocide by a number of parliaments, including the European Parliament — recognition depends on intent, and the intent question is argued by historians, not by committees. 1933–1945 · The Holocaust Six million Jews, and the Roma, the disabled and the political prisoners beside them. The gas chamber was tested first on German patients in the T4 programme, where roughly 250,000 to 300,000 people were killed and, crucially, the paperwork, the false death certificates and the public acceptance were rehearsed. The technique travelled east in the same files. 1937 · Nanjing Weeks of mass killing and rape after the city fell, with figures argued between tens of thousands and hundreds of thousands depending on the source. The dispute over the number has been, for decades, a dispute between states. 1937–38 · Soviet Union The Great Terror, with roughly 700,000 executions recorded in the NKVD's own papers, plus the camps . Quotas were assigned to regions. When the state sets a quota, an obedient man becomes an accomplice by arithmetic. 1940 · Katyn About 22,000 Polish officers and prisoners shot, each with a bullet to the back of the head, in forests that took fifty years to be admitted. The officers were killed by state whose official account was a lie so solid that it divided Europe. 1941 · Jedwabne and Iaşi In Poland, Polish neighbours killed at least 340 Jews in July; in Romania, the Iaşi pogrom killed thousands in June. The Holocaust did not need an imported apparatus everywhere: in places, the local population did the work and the German officers watched. 1942 · Józefów The men of Reserve Police Battalion 101 — middle-aged reservists, not ideological fanatics — shot women and children in a Polish forest. Their commander offered the chance to step out. Most did not. Those who did were not punished. 1943–44 · Bulgaria and Hungary Deportations of Bulgarian Jews were stopped by protests led by Dimitar Peshev; in Hungary, hundreds of thousands were deported after the German occupation, and some were saved by diplomats with stamps. Both facts belong in the same file. 1950s · Kenya British forces fought the Mau Mau insurgency by moving up to 1.5 million Kikuyu into fortified villages and holding suspects in camps where torture was systematic. In 2013 the United Kingdom settled a case brought by survivors for £19.9 million, with a statement of regret — the only court that could rule on most of the victims had already died. 1954–1962 · Algeria French troops used torture as a method, and the method was defended in the name of the Republic's survival. General Pâris de Bollardière asked to be relieved rather than sign it. In 1960, 121 intellectuals and soldiers signed a declaration defending the right to disobey in that war. 1960 · Sharpeville A police line opened fire on a protest against pass laws: 69 dead, most shot in the back. South Africa declared a state of emergency and banned the organisations involved. The photograph of the aftermath is a form of evidence the law cannot refuse. 1965 · Indonesia After a narrative of attempted coup, the army organised the killing of alleged communists: several hundred thousand, up to a million by some estimates. Nobody was punished, and the men who did it still recount it calmly in front of cameras decades later. 1968 · My Lai American soldiers killed 504 civilians, mostly women and children, in a hamlet in Vietnam. The Army's own inquiry found the cover-up. A helicopter crew landed their machine between the troops and the people. The man who did that was called a traitor before he was called a hero. 1970 · Kent State National Guard troops shot into students protesting the war: four dead, nine wounded. The State's own commission called the shooting unjustified. palavrasSubjectivas: A Impotência Ontológica do Discurso Como as palavras falham em alterar a realidade e apenas catalisam a imaginação da mente pensante 1. A Fractura entre o Nome e a Coisa Desde a génese do pensamento filosófico, a humanidade debate-se com uma ilusão persistente: a crença de que a linguagem possui uma força demiúrgica ou mágica, capaz de moldar, reconfigurar ou violar a matéria do universo. Criámos mitos onde mundos nascem da pronúncia de um verbo e onde maldições alteram a biologia dos corpos. Contudo, a física, a biologia e a ontologia rigorosa demonstram rigorosamente o oposto. As palavras são vibrações acústicas de ar deslocado ou traços de pigmento sobre superfícies; elas não possuem carga genética, massa quântica nem força gravitacional para alterar a realidade material. O axioma fundamental sobre o qual assentamos esta reflexão é inequívoco: As palavras não mudam a realidade, elas só potenciam a capacidade de imaginar, de quem tem a capacidade de pensar. Quando um enunciado é proferido, a realidade física permanece absolutamente intocada. O impacto da palavra não ocorre no mundo exterior, mas sim no interior do recetador — no vasto teatro da mente capaz de desconfiar, interpretar e projetar cenários imaginários. É no fosso entre o facto concreto e a projeção mental que a humanidade constrói os seus maiores pesadelos, conflitos e neuroses sociais. 2. A Imutabilidade do Real Perante a Palavra Para testarmos a absoluta impotência da linguagem sobre a matéria, observemos enunciados de diferente amplitude conceitual e o modo como o universo físico responde a cada um deles: Exemplo 1: Impotência sobre a Biologia Enunciado: "Os elefantes têm asas." A Realidade Física: Ao proferir ou escrever esta frase, nenhum paquiderme na savana africana ou indiana sofreu qualquer mutação genética. As suas escápulas não desenvolveram ossos pneumáticos, não surgiram penas ou membranas, nem a força da gravidade deixou de exercer tração sobre o seu corpo de várias toneladas. O elefante permanece rigorosamente sem asas. A palavra falhou em alterar a biologia, mas na mente de quem escuta e pensa, acende-se uma imagem surrealista: um elefante a planar nos céus. Exemplo 2: Impotência sobre o Transcendente Enunciado: "Deus é homossexual." A Realidade Física/Metafísica: O conceito de Divindade — quer seja interpretado como a totalidade do cosmos, a causa primordial ou um ser metafísico — permanece absolutamente inalterado por categorias de orientação sexual humanas criadas no século XIX. Se Deus existe, a Sua natureza substancial não é reconfigurada por uma afirmação verbal; se não existe, o vazio não ganha atributos biológicos. A palavra não toca a essência divina; contudo, na mente do crente ou do teólogo, o enunciado desencadeia uma tempestade de projeções morais, dogmáticas e imaginárias. Exemplo 3: Impotência sobre o Caráter e o Ser Enunciado: "Tu és uma pessoa horrível." A Realidade Pessoal: A estrutura biológica, a memória histórica, as reações químicas e as ações passadas do indivíduo que ouve este julgamento não sofrem qualquer modificação ontológica. A pessoa não se transforma subitamente num monstro físico. A alteração que se segue — a mágoa, a raiva ou a culpa — ocorre exclusivamente porque o recetador, dotado da capacidade de pensar, projeta a hipótese imaginária de "ser horrível" e reage emocionalmente a essa ilusão mental criada por ele próprio. 3. Injúrias, Tabus e o Conflito Criado pela Imaginação O verdadeiro problema humano surge quando nos debruçamos sobre enunciados desenhados para ferir, desumanizar ou insultar. É crucial analisar exemplos ofensivos para compreender a génese do conflito: a ofensa não está na palavra, mas no cenário imaginário que a mente valida como se fosse real. Exemplo Ofensivo 1: A Redução Taxonómica Enunciado: "Tu és um macaco!" Análise Material: O indivíduo atingido por esta injúria não perdeu os seus 46 cromossomas humanos, não viu o seu corpo cobrir-se de estrias pilosas primatas não-humanas, nem a sua espécie biológica mudou para Macaca mulatta ou Pan troglodytes . O seu código genético permanece 100% Homo sapiens . A pessoa **não se transformou num macaco** perante as palavras. O Problema Imaginado: Por que razão este enunciado causa indignação e dor social? Porque a mente humana recupera um histórico social de racismo, hierarquias de desumanização e projeções de inferioridade. A dor não vem de uma mutação física, mas da **capacidade da mente de imaginar a agressão estética e moral** contida no símbolo. Enunciado: "Tu és um parasita inútil, a tua existência é um lixo!" Análise Material: Os órgãos do indivíduo continuam a funcionar, o seu cérebro continua a processar oxigénio e o seu valor biológico permanece inalterado. A palavra "lixo" é uma categoria da gestão de resíduos sólidos humanos, inacessível como estado de matéria biológica viva. O Problema Imaginado: Se o recetador não aplicar o filtro do discernimento racional, a sua imaginação simula a rejeição social, a perda de utilidade e o desprezo dos seus pares, desencadeando respostas neuroquímicas de ansiedade e depressão perante uma pura abstração verbal. 4. A Racionalidade como Filtro entre a Verdade e a Ficção A verdadeira maturidade intelectual e a racionalidade radicam na faculdade de discriminar categoricamente entre o que é faticamente verdadeiro e o que é pura construção fabulada ou falsa, aprendendo a ignorar o falso e a acolher o verdadeiro . "A racionalidade está na capacidade de discernir sobre o que é verdadeiro ou falso, sabendo ignorar o que é falso e reconhecer o que é verdadeiro: Independentemente da cor, todos somos humanos e todos os humanos são animais." Estímulo Verbal (A Palavra) Fato Material / Científico A Armadilha do Imaginário A Resposta Racional "Esta raça é inferior." Todos os humanos partilham 99,9% do genoma; a variação de pigmentação é mera adaptação melânica à radiação UV. Imaginar hierarquias de sangue, superioridade moral e preconceitos históricos. Ignorar o falso: Rejeitar a premissa como erro científico e absurdo biológico. "Nós não somos animais, somos seres divinos purificados." O Homo sapiens é um animal vertebrado, mamífero, da ordem dos primatas, sujeito à biologia e à morte. Imaginar uma separação mística da natureza que justifica a destruição do ecossistema. Reconhecer o verdadeiro: Aceitar a nossa animalidade partilhada e a nossa igualdade biológica. "Tu és uma aberração para a natureza." A diversidade comportamental e biológica é uma constante observada em todas as espécies da biologia. Imaginar-se fora do ordem natural e sentir vergonha existencial. Ignorar o falso: Compreender a palavra como mero ruído ideológico sem adesão à realidade. 5. A Origem do Conflito: O Labirinto da Mente Pensante Se as palavras são impotentes, por que razão guerras foram travadas, duelos foram travados e vidas foram destruídas por causa de insultos ou heresias? A resposta reside inteiramente no **poder da imaginação humana**. A mente humana não é apenas um recetador passivo de dados; é uma máquina de simulação narrativa. Quando alguém ouve uma palavra ofensiva, o cérebro realiza as seguintes etapas em milissegundos: Descodificação Simbólica: O som transforma-se num conceito (ex.: a palavra "macaco" associada a um ser humano). Simulação Imersiva (A Imaginação): A mente constrói uma cena onde o indivíduo é rebaixado, ridicularizado e expulso do grupo social. Em 1867, a grande reforma judiciária portuguesa organiza uma polícia civil sob controlo das autoridades judiciais, com atributos de investigação penal — a matriz de tudo o que a PJ viria a ser. Ao contrário da Guarda Nacional Republicana, que nasce militar e cobre o território, esta polícia nasce administrativa e processual: existe para servir o inquérito, não para patrulhar.
